metadata.title: Checking a Pitch Deck Before It Goes Out.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: what does it actually mean to have Claude check a pitch deck before it goes out? Take the ib-check-deck skill apart — the folder-plus-one-file anatomy, the deliberately dumb linear pipeline, the fixed four-item checklist — name the design choices behind each, and land the carry-out that this reconciles a deck (the same four checks, every slide, every run) rather than proofreading it.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Someone types 'spellcheck' — then hesitates, and corrects it to 'check'. Here's what's actually happening: this isn't proofreading. It's structural reconciliation. Four checks, every slide, every run. Let's take it apart.

beats.act: 1 anatomy — a skill is a folder
beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. A skill is a folder — that's it. One file inside, SKILL.md, written in plain English, spelling out exactly what to look for. Claude reads that file, then follows it. They chose plain English over code because whoever writes the check doesn't need to be a programmer. The trade-off: that file is the whole program — no smarts on top, no drift.

shot.new_visual_element: A folder icon opening to reveal SKILL.md, references/, scripts/; SKILL.md highlighted

production_viz.label: A skill is a folder
production_viz.mechanic: A folder opens on cream to reveal three items: SKILL.md (highlighted in crimson), a references/ folder, a scripts/ folder. An arrow from SKILL.md loops to a small 'Claude reads, then follows it' caption.

beats.narration_text: The pipeline is deliberately dumb: read the file, execute each step in order exactly as written, return the result. No branches unless a step itself asks for one. They optimized for predictability over cleverness — run it on the same deck twice, you get the same answer. That's the whole point of a skill.

shot.new_visual_element: Three-phase pipeline: Read SKILL.md -> Execute steps in order -> Return result

production_viz.label: Input in, output out
production_viz.mechanic: Three cards left to right joined by arrows: 'Read SKILL.md', 'Execute steps in order', 'Return result'. Linear, no branch points drawn.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually on the list — four things, in order. Do the numbers agree across every slide. Does the story match the underlying data. Does the language hold up against IB standards. Is the formatting clean. Run it on the same deck twice, it flags the same four. They chose a fixed checklist over an open-ended review — the win is you know exactly what you got; the cost is anything outside those four does not get looked at.

shot.new_visual_element: Four checklist items with checkmarks: numbers agree, story matches data, language holds up, formatting is clean; a boundary line with 'nothing outside this list' beyond it

production_viz.label: Exactly four checks
production_viz.mechanic: Four checklist rows fill in one at a time with a checkmark: 'Numbers agree across slides', 'Story matches the data', 'Language holds up (IB standard)', 'Formatting is clean'. A dashed boundary line beneath the list, with a faint unlabelled field beyond it captioned 'nothing outside this list'.

beats.narration_text: So here's the carry-out. A skill like this doesn't proofread a deck — it reconciles it: the same four checks, every slide, every run, and nothing outside that checklist gets caught.

props.quote: A skill like this doesn't proofread a deck — it reconciles it: the same four checks, every slide, every run, and nothing outside that checklist gets caught.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste right now into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no skill file, no plugin, no install — that runs the same four-part reconciliation on any deck you already have open. Go deeper: which of the four catches the most on your deck, and what does that pattern say about how your deck actually breaks?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want you to check a pitch deck the same way a professional finish-check would. Here is the deck: [paste your deck's text slide by slide, or attach the file]. Run exactly four checks, in order. (1) Numbers agree across every slide — flag any figure, percentage, growth rate, or dollar amount that doesn't match its own restatement elsewhere in the deck. (2) Narrative matches the data — flag any claim in the prose that the numbers do not support, and any headline that overreaches what the chart shows. (3) Language holds up against investment-banking standards — flag jargon that is used wrong, tone that reads sloppy or promotional, and any claim written stronger than the evidence allows. (4) Formatting is clean — flag inconsistent fonts, misaligned figures, orphaned bullets, and off-brand color use. Return a fix list, grouped by check, with the slide number and the exact fix for each item. Do not flag anything outside those four categories.
